svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. Where the phishing check actually happens
svg.desc: A comparison of two authentication paths under a phishing attack. With a password and a time-based code, the user is the only thing checking the address bar, and anything the user can read out can be relayed to the real site by an attacker. With a FIDO2 credential, four separate parties each apply a check: the browser records the true origin, the browser constrains the relying party identifier to that origin, the authenticator looks for a credential matching the hash of that identifier and finds none on a lookalike domain, and the server verifies both values on arrival. A band below explains that the browser is the enforcement point, which is why the common phrasing that the key checks the domain is a useful shorthand rather than an accurate description.
svg.text: Figure 1: Where the Phishing Check Actually Happens
Both paths ask for a second factor. Only one of them puts the check somewhere a convincing page cannot reach.
The situation in both columns: you are on a lookalike domain that renders perfectly, and you have not noticed.
whether the code arrives by message or by application

g.text: You read the address bar
This is the whole check. There is no second one.
You type the password and the code
Both are values a person can read out, which means
both are values a person can be talked into giving.
The page relays them to the real site immediately
The code is valid for around thirty seconds, and the
attacker needs only a few of those.
A code is a shared secret with a short life, and a short
life is a smaller improvement than it sounds.
This is better than a password alone, and it is phishable.

svg.text: four parties, each applying its own check

g.text: The browser records the true origin
Not the one the page claims. The one it loaded from.
The browser constrains the site identifier to it
A page cannot ask for a credential belonging to a
domain it is not actually served from.
The key looks for a credential matching that hash
On a lookalike domain there is no match, so there is
nothing to sign. Not a refusal. An absence.
The server verifies both values on arrival
The origin and the identifier hash are checked against
what it expects, so a forged client cannot skip step 2.
Nothing replayable ever leaves your device.

svg.text: "The key checks the domain" is a shorthand, and the accurate version tells you more
The key never sees a domain. It sees a hash it was handed, and the browser is what guarantees that hash matches where you really are. That is why the guarantee holds
against a perfect replica of a login page, and why it depends on the client doing its job: a compromised browser, or a client that does not enforce origin correctly,
removes step 1 and step 2. The key is not the whole control. It is the part of the control that cannot be talked into anything.
So the phishing resistance is structural rather than behavioural, which is the entire reason to buy one.
It also tells you exactly which attacks it was never going to stop. That is Figure 2.
